title: How Businesses Can Optimize Payment Costs as They Scale
summary: Payment costs grow with your business. Learn how to understand, manage, and optimize payment costs as you scale.
body_text: As a business grows, its payment costs grow with it. More transactions mean more processing fees. More accounts mean more maintenance costs. More payment methods mean more fee structures to track. What starts as a manageable line item can become a significant operational expense if it is not actively managed. The good news is that scale also brings leverage. Higher transaction volumes unlock better pricing terms. A clearer understanding of your fee structure identifies where costs can be reduced. And the right payment infrastructure makes it possible to grow efficiently rather than expensively. This article covers why payment costs increase as businesses scale, how to understand the different cost components involved, and the most effective strategies for keeping those costs in check without compromising on payment performance. Key Takeaways Payment costs scale with transaction volume, but the relationship is not linear - the right pricing model and provider can reduce your effective rate as you grow Fixed and variable costs behave differently at scale, and understanding both is essential for accurate cost forecasting Common pricing models each have tradeoffs that make them more or less suitable depending on your business stage and transaction profile A long-term payments strategy treats fee optimization as an ongoing discipline, not a one-time exercise Why payment costs increase as businesses grow Payment costs increase with scale for straightforward reasons: more transactions mean more fees, more accounts mean more maintenance costs, and more payment methods mean more fee structures to track and reconcile. But the relationship between scale and cost is not simply linear. A business that grows its transaction volume without revisiting its payment setup often ends up paying more per transaction than necessary. Pricing models that made sense at lower volumes may be suboptimal at higher ones. Fee structures that were manageable with a handful of accounts become unwieldy across dozens of subaccounts. Several specific cost drivers tend to emerge or intensify as businesses scale: Processing fee volume The most direct driver. More transactions mean more processing fees. But the composition of those fees matters as much as the volume. A growing business with a shifting payment method mix - more premium credit cards, more cross-border transactions, more high-value orders - may see its effective processing rate rise even if the headline rate stays the same. Account and maintenance fees Businesses that grow through platform structures or multi-entity setups accumulate accounts over time. Accounts that fall below minimum activity thresholds attract dormant account fees. At Xendit, a monthly minimum fee of USD 50 applies to dormant and inactive accounts. Having clear visibility of your portfolio of subaccounts, can help prevent unmanaged dormancy from becoming a material cost. Legacy API maintenance Businesses still operating on older API infrastructure may be subject to additional maintenance fees. At Xendit, a monthly maintenance fee of USD 250 applies to merchants using the legacy API. Migrating to current API versions eliminates this cost. Chargeback and dispute fees As transaction volume grows, so does chargeback exposure unless fraud prevention scales in parallel. Each chargeback carries a dispute fee - at Xendit, a chargeback dispute fee of USD 25 applies. Understanding how you can minimize chargebacks, can help to reduce this. Attempt fees on failed transactions At Xendit, a processing fee applies to every transaction attempt regardless of outcome. For businesses with growing transaction volumes, a high decline rate amplifies this cost. Improving authorization rates becomes more financially important as volume increases. Read also: What Is a Chargeback Fee? A Complete Guide for Businesses Common pricing models used by payment providers Your pricing model determines how your processing fees scale with volume. Understanding the most common models - and their tradeoffs - is essential for evaluating whether your current model is still appropriate as your business grows. Flat rate pricing. A single blended rate applies to every transaction regardless of payment method or transaction size. Simple to manage and predict, but often less cost-effective at higher volumes because the rate does not reflect the actual cost profile of your transactions. Interchange-plus pricing. The network and issuing bank fees are passed through at cost, and the provider adds a fixed markup on top. More transparent and typically more cost-effective at higher volumes, because the markup is the only negotiable component and it is visible separately. Tiered pricing. Transactions are categorized into tiers - typically qualified, mid-qualified, and non-qualified - with different rates for each tier. Less transparent than interchange-plus because tier classification can be opaque. Often less favorable than it appears when analyzed in detail. Subscription or membership pricing. A fixed monthly fee provides access to processing at near-cost network rates, plus a small per-transaction fee. Highly cost-effective for high-volume businesses where the monthly fee is outweighed by the savings on per-transaction rates. Read also: A Complete Guide to Payment Fees: What Your Business Is Actually Paying For Building a long-term payments strategy Payment cost optimization is most effective when it is treated as an ongoing discipline rather than a periodic exercise. The businesses that manage payment costs most effectively build a payment strategy that evolves with their growth rather than reacting to costs after they have already accumulated. A long-term payment strategy includes several components: A clear owner for payment operations Someone in your organization - typically in finance, operations, or a dedicated payments function - should be responsible for monitoring payment costs, managing provider relationships, and identifying optimization opportunities. Without clear ownership, payment costs tend to drift upward unmanaged. Regular cost reviews Schedule a payment cost review at least quarterly. Review your effective processing rate, account portfolio, chargeback rate, authorization rate, and provider terms. Compare against the previous period and against benchmarks appropriate for your business type and volume. A provider relationship built on transparency Your payment provider should be a partner in cost optimization, not an obstacle. A good provider relationship includes open communication about fees, proactive advice on how to reduce costs, and willingness to revisit commercial terms as your business grows. Infrastructure that scales without friction The right payment infrastructure allows your business to add payment methods, markets, and transaction volume without adding proportionate complexity or cost. Evaluating your payment infrastructure not just for current needs but for where your business is heading is part of a long-term payments strategy. Grow efficiently with Xendit Xendit provides payment infrastructure designed to support businesses at every stage of growth across multiple markets. Here is how Xendit supports cost-efficient payment operations as your business scales: Transparent fee reporting Every fee: processing, refund, dispute, platform, and account fees appears as a clear line item in your Xendit dashboard, giving your finance team the visibility needed to manage costs accurately at any scale Account portfolio management Your Xendit dashboard gives you visibility across master accounts and subaccounts, making it straightforward to identify dormant accounts and take action before fees accumulate Wide payment method coverage Accept credit and debit cards, bank transfers, e-wallets, virtual accounts, QR payments, and other local payment methods across multiple markets - allowing your payment mix to evolve as your business grows without adding provider complexity Fraud detection built in Xendit's fraud detection system reduces chargeback exposure and improves authorization rates, directly reducing the per-transaction cost of processing at volume Multi-market infrastructure For businesses expanding across Southeast Asia and beyond, Xendit provides payment infrastructure through licensed entities in each market, reducing the compliance and operational complexity of cross-border payment operations Ready to build payment operations that scale efficiently? Create a Xendit account and start with transparent fee reporting from day one. Frequently Asked Questions Why do payment costs increase as businesses grow? Payment costs increase with scale because more transactions generate more processing fees, more accounts generate more maintenance costs, and a higher volume of chargebacks and refunds generates more dispute and refund fees. The composition of your transaction mix also matters - a shift toward higher-cost payment methods or more cross-border transactions can raise your effective rate even if your headline pricing stays the same. What is the difference between fixed and variable payment costs? Variable costs scale with transaction volume, processing fees, chargeback fees, and refund fees are the primary examples. Fixed costs apply regardless of volume, monthly maintenance fees for legacy API access and monthly minimum fees on dormant accounts are fixed costs. Understanding the distinction helps your finance team forecast accurately and identify where optimization has the most leverage. What account related fees apply at Xendit? At Xendit, a monthly minimum fee of USD 50 applies to dormant and inactive accounts. A monthly maintenance fee of USD 250 applies to merchants still using the legacy API. How does improving my authorization rate reduce costs? A higher authorization rate means more of your payment attempts result in successful transactions. This reduces the volume of attempt fees paid on declined transactions and recovers revenue from customers who would otherwise abandon their purchase after a decline. At scale, even a modest improvement in authorization rate delivers a compounding financial benefit. How can I reduce chargeback fees as my business grows? The most effective approaches are improving fraud detection to reduce fraudulent transactions, maintaining clear billing descriptors and refund policies to reduce friendly fraud, and responding to disputes quickly with strong evidence. At Xendit, a chargeback dispute fee of USD 25 applies on each dispute, so reducing chargeback volume has a direct impact on this cost line. How does Xendit support payment cost optimization at scale? title: Prevention is Strength: 5 Health Behaviors Men Should Start Today
summary: Men in the US underutilize preventative care, but early prevention matters. Omada recommends five preventative health behaviors to help manage men's health.
body_text: June 18, 2026 Prevention is Strength: 5 Health Behaviors Men Should Start Today By Kevin Masci, Pharm D and Todd Norwood, PT, DPT, FACHE This edition covers: Men in the U.S. are underutilizing preventive care How male gender norms impact health behavior Why early prevention matters for men For all the advances in medicine and technology, one stubborn truth remains: men in the US still underutilize preventive care. In a culture that often/many times celebrates toughness and self-reliance, many men wait until symptoms are undeniable or a crisis forces their hand. These patterns can ultimately increase the risk of heart attacks and strokes , chronic pain and disability, and/or reduce quality of life and longevity. Cardiovascular risk, in particular, often builds quietly for years before it becomes visible. As clinicians, we see the downstream consequences of delayed preventive care every day. We also see a paradox: men who are disciplined, data-driven, and proactive in nearly every other area of life often avoid their own health maintenance. This isn't about a lack of intelligence or discipline. The barriers are real: fear of what a diagnosis might mean, schedules that leave no room for provider visits, and a lifetime of cultural messages that frame help-seeking as weakness. We know men can engage in prevention, and we believe it’s time to change the narrative and reframe prevention as an expression of strength. Men Avoid Using Preventive Health Services Survey after survey show that many men avoid the doctor and skip routine screenings, even when they’re recommended. A Cleveland Clinic survey found that 72% would rather do household chores than go to the doctor, and only half would consider getting regular health screenings. Men are less likely than women to use preventive services such as blood pressure checks, cholesterol testing, and routine exams. These patterns show up in outcomes: men develop many cardiometabolic conditions earlier and have shorter average lifespans. Underneath the statistics are ordinary decisions that impact health down the line: ignoring routine doctor visits and labwork, shrugging off chest discomfort, toughing out back pain, or pushing through low mood and stress with no support. Gender norms about toughness, self-sufficiency, and “not making a fuss” push many men to downplay symptoms, assume problems will “work themselves out,” or wait for a dramatic wake-up call. By then, the window for easy intervention has often passed. The irony is that in other domains such as sports, vehicles and grooming, those same men are often meticulous, scheduled, and proactive. The Juxtaposition of Common Male Habits and Preventive Health Behavior Many men already practice the underlying skills that preventive health requires. We already follow schedules, monitor performance, and maintain the things that matter to us. The opportunity is to direct some of that same attention toward ourselves. Not because it will be easy, but because the infrastructure is already there. Your stats, not just your rosters If you're into fantasy football, you probably know your roster cold. You track rushing yards, red-zone targets, snap counts, and injury reports, and you adjust lineups by the hour on game day. Now consider a few relevant stats for your own health: Do you know your last blood pressure reading as well as your QB’s completion percentage? Could you name your latest A1c or cholesterol levels as easily as your WR1’s yards after catch? When a star running back tweaks a hamstring, fantasy managers are on it immediately, checking reports, planning substitutions, and monitoring recovery. When it comes to tracking your own health numbers, the stakes are much higher. A bad number means something about your body, not just your lineup, and that is part of what makes this harder. But the core habit of paying attention to data, noticing trends, and acting on what you find is directly transferable. The question is whether you are willing to apply it to yourself. Engine gauges and warning lights When the “check engine” light glows on your dashboard, you might not know exactly what’s wrong, but you know it’s worth getting checked before you’re stranded on the side of the highway. Your body has gauges and warning lights too, such as: Blood pressure creeping up New chest tightness when you climb stairs Numbness or burning in your feet Knee or back pain that keeps returning Ignoring those signals doesn’t make you tougher, it just makes the eventual breakdown more likely and more expensive physically, emotionally, and financially. Getting checked out is not overreacting. It is reading the gauges and adjusting course before a manageable problem becomes a serious one. Shaving, barber visits, and routine care as a standard commitment For many men, grooming is non‑negotiable. You shave regularly without overthinking it. You book barber appointments on a schedule and keep them. You sit in the chair, trust the professional, and walk out feeling sharper. Preventive care can work the same way: Primary care visits and screenings are standing appointments, not last‑minute emergencies Honest conversations vs. the partial truths many men admit to in surveys Medication refills and lab checks are routine maintenance, like replacing blades before they dull You already know how to show up consistently for people and systems you trust like barbers, trainers, coaches, coworkers; the goal is to extend the same consistency to your own healthcare. Why Early Prevention Matters for Men Cardiovascular disease develops over time Heart disease remains the leading cause of death for men in the United States. Diabetes and prediabetes are common and often silent in early stages, especially when routine glucose or A1c checks are skipped. These conditions often build over years through elevated blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol , weight gain, rising glucose, and lifestyle patterns that go unaddressed. In fact, men are likely to exhibit elevated cholesterol levels a full decade before women. When these signals are caught early, nutrition changes, targeted activity, and medications can dramatically reduce risk. By the time a heart attack, stroke, or severe neuropathy appears, damage has already accumulated. Prevention is about acting earlier in the timeline, while the system is still flexible and responsive. Ignoring aches and pains can create chronic musculoskeletal issues In the physical therapy clinic, we often see men who have powered through back, shoulder, or knee pain for months or years. What started as a manageable issue has evolved into chronic pain, compensation patterns and lost function. This is a pattern consistent with how under-treated musculoskeletal problems contribute to disability and cost. They come in only when pain interferes with work, sleep, or the activities they love. Contrast that with how you’d treat a strange noise coming from your truck or flickering light in your living room. You might let it go for a short while, but you are aware that it could be the symptom of a larger issue that shouldn’t be left unaddressed. Listening to pain is not giving in. It is reading the signal and acting on it while options are still wide open. Mental health is a bigger problem than the numbers show Nearly 1 in 10 men experience depression or anxiety , and this figure almost certainly understates the true prevalence when subclinical distress, untreated substance use, and the well-documented tendency of men to underreport symptoms are factored in. Yet many men have absorbed the message that feeling overwhelmed is a personal failure and that seeking help is “unmanly.” This results in lower rates of mental health treatment, higher rates of suicide and substance-related death, and suffering that did not have to reach crisis level. But consider where men already open up and discuss their emotions honestly: in the barber chair, at the gym, on the golf course, and in the group chat. This same openness doesn’t always make it into the exam room or therapy office, where effective help is available. Even our favorite professional athletes, including some of the all time greats, work with sports psychologists to support their emotional and mental well-being. Reframing mental health support as part of regular maintenance, i.e. fine-tuning the system, not “fixing what’s broken,” can make the first step feel less like an admission and more like a decision. Five Preventive Health Behaviors to Start Today What does it look like to put all this into practice? Think of these five areas as the “key players” on your health roster, you don’t need to start all five at once. The evidence on behavior change is consistent: building one habit, making it sustainable, and adding from there works better than a full overhaul. Start with the area that has the most room to improve, and build from there. 1. Know and track your numbers Learn your key metrics: blood pressure, cholesterol, A1c or fasting glucose, waist circumference, and weight trend. These are all critical markers tied to future cardiovascular and metabolic risk. Treat them like season-long stats. Track them on your phone or patient portal and watch how they respond to changes in activity, nutrition, sleep, and medications. Work with your clinician to set targets and a plan, the same way you’d map out a fantasy draft strategy or weight training plan. 2. Move with purpose, not just intensity Mix strength training, mobility, and cardio rather than relying on occasional “weekend warrior” efforts. A balanced approach supports your metabolic, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal health more effectively than sporadic intensity. Think of it like maintaining a car—performance depends on regular maintenance, not irregular trips to the mechanic. A simple, research-backed starting point: Walk more, add two days of resistance training each week, and build gradually from there. What matters most is consistency over time, not how hard you push on any single day. If you’re dealing with persistent pain or a specific injury, consider an evaluation with a physical therapist or qualified clinician before activity becomes more limited. 3. Treat pain as a signal, not a test If pain is persistent, worsening, or limiting the way you move, get it evaluated; early intervention can often prevent chronic pain and disability. Early physical therapy or medical care can keep a small issue from turning into surgery, chronic pain, or missed work. Listening to pain is not “giving in”; it’s reading the gauges and adjusting course. 4. Invest in metabolic and lifestyle health Build a pattern of eating that prioritizes whole foods, fiber, and lean protein most days, and minimizes added sugars. Aim for regular sleep and consistent movement rather than perfection; both are linked to better cardiometabolic outcomes. If you drink alcohol, drink it in moderation and avoid tobacco; both drive risk for cardiovascular disease and several cancers. If you have access to a health coaching program, whether through your employer or health plan, look into it. Lifestyle support between doctor’s visits helps keep your progress in check. You don't need a total life overhaul. Small, consistent upgrades are like weekly waiver-wire moves: modest in the moment, powerful over a season. 5. Shift from crisis management to purposeful prevention Put annual checkups, dental visits, and key screenings on the calendar the way you schedule haircuts, oil changes, or fantasy drafts. Show up prepared: know your questions, share your concerns, and be honest about what’s working and what isn’t. Honesty improves the quality of care and is exactly what many men say they struggle with in surveys. Think of your clinician as part of your “coaching staff,” not just an emergency technician. Be Strong for Yourself, Not Just Everyone Else At its core, this is a conversation about what strength really means. Stoicism and silence in the face of warning signs may look tough on the surface, but they often lead to more pain, more limitation, and fewer healthy years. Strength can mean something different than what many of us were taught: Paying attention to your own “stats” and acting on them Respecting the warning lights instead of taping over the dashboard Showing up for routine care as reliably as you show up for the people and commitments you value Being honest with yourself and with your care team about what you’re feeling and what you need. We know that managing your own health is not always easy, but that’s not a reason to avoid it. Rather, it’s a reason to start smaller and build more deliberately than you might think necessary. We know life will always throw challenges our way. Prevention is about entering those challenges with as much capacity, reserve, and resilience as possible. title: The Next Chapter at Inspectify
body_text: For Everyone The Next Chapter at Inspectify June 9, 2026 Historically, I’ve written a “Year In Review” at the end of each year to highlight the accomplishments of our team over the years, but last month something quite significant happened that I’ve decided to take a minute and reflect on where we’ve come from and more importantly, where we are going. ‍ I’m so humbled and proud to share that as of last month, Inspectify hit positive cash flow for the first time in company history. The last seven years have been a rollercoaster to put it lightly, but over the last 18 months, we have hit an inflection point that has resulted in over 350% growth of revenues and culminated with us hitting double digit EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization) margin last month. This milestone makes us “Default Alive”, a premise that was drilled into us during our early days at YCombinator, a time which seems like a lifetime ago. Most importantly, we now have complete control over our path forward and will be even more aggressive in terms of how we grow our offering and expand our market share from here. For my own benefit, I’ve taken the last few weeks to really reflect on the last seven years and by doing so I’ve compartmentalized that journey over three chapters. ‍ Chapter 1: Formation (2019 - 2022) The first Chapter of Inspectify starts like most early stage tech companies; a lot of trying, a lot of failing and our first taste of product market fit. It shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone that the first product and business model we built failed in epic fashion. The idea was simple: build great home inspection software, give it away to home inspectors for free to start capturing a massive, proprietary dataset on properties in the country. Our first app, HIA, short for Home Inspections App (yup, I’m THAT good at branding) was a great MVP, but we failed because of distribution. Home inspectors were quick to realize the classic adage that if the product is free, then you are the product. More importantly, we were solution-seeking, not problem-solving. Back to the drawing board we went. ‍ I then reflected hard on my experience at a Flyhomes, where I managed diligence (inspections, appraisals, etc.) for the homes we were buying with our clients. Operationally, I had to build a team of people to simply manage all the vendors, standardize the outputs and ultimately make a decision on the property. Bluntly, it was a major pain in the ass and did not generate any revenue for the business – bingo , that’s my pain point. We quickly built an MVP, signed up multiple customers and started generating revenue in January 2020. I then made a pretty pitch deck and set up 20+ meetings with early stage VCs in Feb 2020… and then the entire country shut down due to the Covid outbreak and all VCs closed their doors to focus on keeping their existing portfolio afloat… impeccable timing on my end. ‍ Somehow over the next two months we were able to convince Brad, Dalton and Aaron at YCombinator to give us a shot and joined the S20 batch. There was just one catch; they made me bring on a technical co-founder given they had so little faith in my coding skills (still slightly offended). Over a 48 hour period and a few convos I was able to convince Denis to take the plunge and join me on this crazy journey; he joined Inspectify on my 33rd birthday, best birthday ever. We iterated even faster during YC on the offering and were able to piece together a seed round in Fall of 2020 and start building out a small team. ‍ Up until that time, we were able to grow modestly through selling to brokerages and various Proptech companies around the real estate transaction. Then, through a friend, I got connected with Invitation Homes and we were introduced to the red hot Single Family Rental industry (SFR). What happened next was our first real taste of product market fit. Over the first six months of 2021 we grew 10X and accepted a term sheet for our Series A from Kurt and the team at Nine Four Ventures; a group that passed on our Seed round, but, true to their word, busted their ass to make intros and help us grow even though they weren’t on the cap table yet. We closed our Series A in late 2021 and proceeded to grow another 250% over the next six months of 2022 and our team ballooned to over 85 team members to keep pace with that growth. ‍ Chapter 2: Reset and Stability (2023 - 2026) The next Chapter began with something that anyone who was in real estate over the past 5 years knows all too well. In late February 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine triggering a stark market sell off, collapsing the venture capital ecosystem overnight while rising inflation spiked to 8% causing the Federal Reserve overnight to begin hiking interest rates. The end result? Our growth stalled and over the next six months our revenue declined by more than 50%. Given the uncertainty in our ability to continue to fund the business, and the overhiring we had done over the past 12 months, we had to let go of a large portion of our team to ensure the company’s survival. This was and continues to be one of my biggest failures as a CEO and fundamentally changed how I’ve thought about growing the business since. ‍ With the company reset, we started clawing ourselves back; doing so by beginning to diversify our customer base which fundamentally changed the direction of the business. In 2023 alone, we launched our first clients in property management, construction lending, and insurance and began building a brand as the platform for any kind of property visit. Up to this point, our vision for the business was purely centered around the real estate transaction and building a sizable business by obtaining Uber-level marketshare, but our diversification dramatically changed that thinking. We actively re-tooled our platform to handle any and all needs of capturing data around real estate and were able to add enough new customers to hold revenues flat year over year in 2023. ‍ While we were rebuilding our customer base in 2023 and into 2024, we also started making significant investments into our operating model to improve efficiencies and learn from our mistakes in 2022. As we expanded customer segments that were higher volume / lower cost property visits (i.e. insurance, mortgage servicing, etc.), it would be critical for us to be able to fulfill inspections at a much lower cost and faster speed. In early 2023, we rolled out Automated Scheduling (AS),, our back office engine to coordinate inspections autonomously. By the end of 2023, 50% of our inspections went through AS, by the end of 2024, we hit 80% of our inspections. Most importantly, entering 2025 we were completing twice as many inspections as we were before the downturn with a third of the headcount on our operations. ‍ We entered 2025 with a strong operational foundation and a large new market to go after. In early 2025, we changed from defense to offense with the acquisitions of Aloft and Joule Homes and, with those, the expansion into two more segments, appraisals / valuations and home energy audits. Over the next six months, we aggressively integrated and retooled the new teams and tech we acquired and finished the year growing nearly 80% in revenue. Additionally, after years of development, we began the rollout of Voxier, our computer vision / AI layer that allowed us to further automate the inspection workflow and objectively improve the quality of the data output. ‍ During that expansion in 2025, we began exploring our next capital raise (Series B) and found the almost blind polarization toward “AI native companies” as a significant threat to our business if we were to be dependent on venture capital over the coming years. In September, we set a target to hit profitability by April of 2026 and do so by growing the top line and improving unit economics with further application of automation through our platform. Since that target was set, we doubled revenue, we grew gross margin nearly 20% (percentage points), and delivered a 12% EBITDA margin in May. ‍ Chapter 3: Building the Human Layer of Real Estate (2026+) This brings us to today. As I think about the direction we are heading over the next seven years, it is the culmination of everything that has happened over the past seven. ‍ First, let’s start with what is our greatest strength and most important characteristic of our platform. We have built the fastest, most robust, and most efficient platform for capturing physical data on real estate today. For example, we have doubled the number of visits to properties we do per month in the last five months and our SLAs and unit economics have only improved. I’m biased, but I’m bullish that we have by far the best infrastructure for getting someone to and into a property at scale and have never been more confident that we can expand 100X and the system will absorb the demand. ‍ Second, the market size in front of us feels limitless. It’s almost weekly now that we have a new customer use case land on our desk to handle the physical visit to a property. Installing lockboxes for property managers? Sure, let’s figure it out. Inspecting roofs after large catastrophic events for insurance carriers? Easy. Taking marketing photos for real estate listings? Consider it done. What we have found is there is an enormous addressable market for physical visits to real estate and estimate that there are multiple billions of occurrences every year in the US across residential and commercial real estate. ‍ Finally, timing is in our favor. With the rapid adoption of AI over the past two years, the traditional SaaS model has been completely upended and, while I don’t think SaaS is going away by any means, it creates a world where more and more companies are taking a harder look at their workflows and the software they are paying for and asking if they can replace it with something homegrown and bespoke. For us, it creates a massive opportunity to become the connective tissue between our customers' tech stacks and their physical assets. To put it another way, to become the human layer for all real estate asset classes and all stages of a properties lifecycle. ‍ Today marks a new day for Inspectify. One where we can aggressively reinvest our profits back into the platform to accelerate growing market share, product expansion, and development of our team. It’s been a hell of ride over the past seven years and we wouldn’t be here today if not for our team (both current and past) who have grinded through one of the worst five years in real estate, our customers , who continue to put their trust into our platform, and our investors who continue to invest and support us when everyone else was running the other direction. ‍ Since I started this journey in 2019, I’ve acquired a few more grey hairs, a lot more wrinkles, a lot of lessons learned, and exponentially more conviction that we are building a platform that will change how real estate is built, bought, and managed for decades to come. ‍
